Surface integral equation methods are advantageous for simulating electromagnetic wave scattering by three-dimensional obstacles.
SIE methods reduce the dimension of the problem by discretizing only the scatterer's surface.
SIE methods are robust for high-frequency scattering problems.
The cost of setting up discretized dense linear systems is high due to the evaluation of highly oscillatory magnetic and electric dipole surface integral operators.
The computational complexity of evaluating such integrals depends on the incident wave frequency, the size, and the shape of the obstacles.
The paper discusses a surface integral reformulation of the scattering problem involving highly oscillatory physical densities.
Efficient evaluation methods are discussed for smooth three-dimensional scatterers with diameters much larger than the incident wavelength.
The exterior Maxwell equations for the radiating electric and magnetic fields are given by curl Es - ikHs = 0 and curl Hs + ikEs = 0.
The radiating fields satisfy the Silver-Müller radiation condition, ensuring they behave as outgoing spherical waves at infinity.
The radiating solution Hs can be represented using the fundamental solution of the Helmholtz equation and surface integrals over the scatterer's boundary.
The farfield pattern H∞ is crucial for inverse scattering theory and radar cross section calculations.
For a plane wave incident on a perfectly conducting obstacle, the tangential part of the total electric field must vanish on the surface.
The Stratton-Chu formulae are used to relate the incident and scattered fields and compute the scattered magnetic field and its farfield pattern.
The magnetic dipole operator is used to define the weakly-singular surface integral equation for the unknown density function v.
The exact treatment of singularities is crucial for handling the highly oscillatory nature of the integrals in high-frequency scattering.
Algorithms for efficient evaluation of high-frequency electromagnetic scattering integrals are still a challenge, especially for non-convex obstacles.
The asymptotic approximation approach may not be efficient or suitable for non-convex obstacle scattering.
Compression techniques, such as those used with wavelet bases, are proposed for efficient simulations of non-convex obstacle scattering.
The paper references several works on efficient algorithms for low to medium frequency scattering, but practical realizations for very high-frequency problems are not efficient.
The paper highlights the need for new algorithms to facilitate efficient simulations for three-dimensional non-convex obstacles with diameters much larger than the incident wavelength.
